source_text: Accedit ad testimonium antiquitatis subsecuta posteritas formam originis de titulis huius quoque temporis praeferens, per quos signatum est, cui idolo et cui superstitioni utriusque generis ludi notarentur. Megalenses enim et Apollinares, item Cereales et Neptunales et Latiares et Florales in commune celebrantur; reliqui ludorum de natalibus et sollemnibus regum et publicis prosperitatibus et municipalibus festis superstitionis causas habent. inter quos etiam priuatorum memoriis legatariae editiones parentant, id quoque secundum institutionis antiquitatem. nam et a primordio bifariam ludi censebantur, sacri et funebres id est deis nationum et mortuis. sed de idololatria nihil differt apud nos, sub quo nomine et titulo, dum ad eosdem spiritus perueniat, quibus renuntiamus. licebit mortuis, licebit deis suis faciant, perinde mortuis suis ut diis faciunt; una condicio partis utriusque est, una idololatria, una renuntiatio nostra aduersus idololatrian.
thought_title: Titles of the games reveal their idolatrous origin
orientation: Tertullian has just shown that the first Roman games were instituted for idols, and now he argues that the names and occasions of later games continue to mark them as idolatrous.
pass_a_gloss: To the testimony of antiquity there is added the following posterity, which displays the form of the origin in the titles of this present time also, through which titles it has been marked for which idol and for which superstition the games of each kind were assigned. For the Megalensian and Apollinarian games, likewise the Cerealian and Neptunalian and Latin and Florian games are celebrated in common; the remaining games have causes of superstition from the birthdays and solemnities of kings and public prosperities and municipal festivals. Among these also legacy editions perform funeral rites for the memories of private persons, this also according to the antiquity of the institution. For also from the beginning the games were reckoned in two ways, sacred and funereal, that is for the gods of the nations and for the dead. But as regards idolatry it makes no difference among us under what name and title, provided that it reaches to the same spirits which we renounce. It is permitted that they do them for the dead, it is permitted that they do them for their gods, in the same way they do them for their dead as for gods; one condition belongs to each part, one idolatry, one renunciation of ours against idolatry.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'games' for ludi, not 'public games' or 'entertainments'.
The glossary requires 'idolatry' for idololatria, the root sin Tertullian is tracing.
This refers to the baptismal renunciation of the devil and his works, a key term in the treatise.
Literal rendering of the phrase; 'nations' preserves the biblical idiom for pagans, matching Tertullian's usage.
Literal rendering; these are games funded by bequests in wills for the dead, hence 'legacy' keeps the legal sense.

choices.english: one condition belongs to each part
choices.why: Literal rendering of condicio as 'condition' or 'status'; both sacred and funereal games share the same standing.
rejected: the same case for each kind

pass_b_english: Later generations add their own testimony to that of antiquity. Even in the titles of the present age they display the pattern of the origin, for the titles mark to which idol and to which superstition the games of each kind were assigned. The Megalensian and Apollinarian games are celebrated publicly, and likewise the Cerealian, Neptunalian, Latin, and Floralian games. The remaining games have their grounds in superstition: the birthdays and solemnities of kings, public prosperities, and municipal festivals. Among these, bequests also perform funeral rites for the memories of private individuals, and this too follows the antiquity of the institution. For from the beginning games were reckoned in two ways: sacred and funereal, that is, for the gods of the nations and for the dead.

But as far as we are concerned, it makes no difference to the charge of idolatry under what name or title they are held, as long as they reach the same spirits whom we renounce. Let them hold them for the dead; let them hold them for their gods. They do for their dead just as they do for their gods. One condition belongs to each part: one idolatry, one renunciation of ours against idolatry.

problems.why: 'Legacy editions' sounds like modern publishing; likely means 'heirs' or 'bequests' staging funeral games.
problems.fix: Replace with: 'heirs by bequest' or 'those who inherit'

fixed: Changed 'legacy editions' to 'bequests': source 'legatariae editiones' means editions or productions funded by legacy/bequest, i.e., funeral games paid for by a bequest; 'legacy editions' is a false friend. 'Bequests' fits the sentence: 'Among these, bequests also perform funeral rites...'

polish.changed: Clarified that 'legacy editions' means bequests staging funeral rites, smoothed sentence order, and made the contrast between pagan practice and Christian renunciation easier to follow aloud.
